title: Concavity, convexity, and inflection points
section: Curve Sketching ▷ Properties of the second derivative
terms: concave up; convex function; concave down; inflection point; second-derivative sign.

exposition.text:
′′
For twice differentiable functions, f ≥ 0 on an interval implies convexity, also called concavity
up; slopes are nondecreasing and the graph lies above each tangent. The opposite inequalities
describe concavity down. Strict positivity or negativity provides strict curvature, but a zero
second derivative at one point alone supplies little information.
An inflection point is a point on the graph where concavity changes across the point. Possi-
′′
ble candidates satisfy f = 0 or failure of the second derivative, but these conditions are not
sufficient. Verify the change of concavity. An inflection point need not be stationary, and a
stationary point need not be an extremum. These distinctions are frequent conceptual traps.
Without assuming differentiability, convexity means f ((1 − t)x + ty) ≤ (1 − t)f(x) + tf(y)
for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1. Thus the graph lies below its chords. Secant slopes on successive intervals are
nondecreasing, which gives both upper and lower bounds from known function values.

question.text:
A convex function f : [−1, 1] → R satisfies f(−1) = 2, f(0) = 0, and f(1) = 2. What is the
sharp interval of possible values of f(1/2)?
(A) [0, 1] (B) [−1, 1] (C) [−2, 2] (D) [0, 2] (E) [−1, 2]

solution.text:
The chord from 0 to 1 gives f (1/2) ≤ 1. Monotonicity of secant slopes gives
[f (0) − f(−1)]/(0 + 1) ≤ [f(1/2) − f(0)]/(1/2), so f(1/2) ≥ −1. Both bounds, and
every intermediate value, are attained by the piecewise linear interpolant through the four
stated points; its successive slopes are −2, 2t, 4 − 2t, nondecreasing exactly when −1 ≤ t ≤ 1.
